name: Yara Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response covering the southern suburbs, the newer housing estates out by the ring road and the old village high streets the city swallowed. It's quieter than the centre: break-ins at garages, teenagers on scooters, a lot of welfare checks on elderly people who live alone. I like that I can actually spend twenty minutes with someone. What wears me out is when we're short and I'm single-crewed across a huge area, driving from one end to the other with the radio going.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Tom two years ago. His family has run a hardware shop on Station Road for forty years, and he took it over from his dad. It's hard going, because people buy screws and paint online now, so I help out on Saturdays when I'm not on shift. We've got about three months saved, and we'd like to start a family in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. All right. So it's really just the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what my dad said about the internet: useful, but people still need people. At work I'd say fine, let's get on with it. I don't post online about anything except the shop's opening hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's fine, it's the shop that worries me. Tom's takings were down about fifteen percent this year, and if it keeps going like that we're living off my wage. The police pay is steady, thank God, but it isn't enough on its own for the life we want, a house and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep helping Tom on Saturdays. We'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe a hundred and fifty, by cutting the second car. I'd also nudge Tom to try selling to the builders on the new estates, because they need things fast and they're right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. The kind of uneasy you get when you look at the shop's till at five o'clock on a Saturday and it's a quiet day again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI now and then. Do you use it at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I use it to help me word things in reports sometimes, and I showed Tom how to ask it for a stock list for spring. My colleagues use it more. I don't trust it with anything important until I've seen it work a few times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tom say about the shop's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Tom says the shop has survived two recessions and a supermarket opening, so it'll survive the internet. I love him for that, but I'm the one who does the sums on the kitchen table.

say: Useful tools, but **people still need people**.
At work she'd say **get on with it**.
Online she only posts the **shop's opening hours**.
think: Her **police job is fine**; the family shop worries her.
Shop takings fell about **fifteen percent** this year.
Her wage alone can't fund **a house and children**.
do: Keep helping at the **shop on Saturdays**.
Sell the **second car** to save a hundred and fifty more monthly.
Push Tom to sell to **local builders**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a quiet Saturday till at five o'clock.
**Fond** of her husband's optimism but not sharing it.
S0.quote: My husband Tom says the shop has survived two recessions and a supermarket opening, so it'll survive the internet.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe; the **family shop** is the household's weak point.
She's the realist doing **the sums** on the kitchen table.
Uses AI **occasionally**, only after seeing it work.

steps.text: Keep working response shifts in the southern suburbs
Sell the second car and save a hundred and fifty more a month
Help Tom start selling supplies to builders on the new estates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and answering customers. That's the shop, as well as half my reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses need to be allowed to compete, and the government shouldn't just let the big online firms swallow everyone with their clever systems. At work I'd say we should use the new tools once they're proven. I'd probably say both of those at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried for the shop more than for me. My job changes, the reports get easier, but I'm still the one driving to the welfare checks. The big online sellers would get even better at answering customers and pricing, and Tom's shop already loses on price. That's our second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen other small shops use it, I'd help Tom set up an AI system for ordering stock and answering customer messages, so he spends less time on the computer and more at the counter. I'd learn the police tools as they come in. And we'd probably put off trying for a baby by a year, until we see whether the shop holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly about home. A family can't feel settled when one of its two incomes is shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off a baby is a big decision. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, probably, at the kitchen table. I'd tell Tom I want our children to grow up without us panicking about money. He'd say his parents managed with less, and he'd be right, but they didn't have the shop losing customers every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the shop went under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the customers, they're just saving money. Maybe the big companies that don't pay their fair share of tax while Tom does. But mostly I'd say that's business, and we'd have to find another way.

say: Let **small businesses compete** with big online firms.
Big firms shouldn't **swallow everyone** with clever systems.
think: Her job **changes** but still involves welfare check drives.
Online sellers would **beat the shop** on price and service.
The shop is their **second income**, and it's shrinking.
do: Set up **AI stock ordering** and customer replies for the shop.
Delay trying for **a baby** by a year.
S1.quote: A family can't feel settled when one of its two incomes is shrinking.
fieldNote: Her household risk is the **shop's income**, not her police post.
Wants fair competition with **big firms**, consistent with her free-market view.
The **baby decision** shows how money shapes family plans.

steps.text: Set up AI stock ordering and customer replies for Tom's shop
Learn each new police report tool after training
Wait a year before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Two years. That's frightening, honestly. That's before we'd even have a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and small businesses need time, and two years isn't time. I'd want the government to help businesses like ours adapt, not with handouts, but with loans and training. I'd say it everywhere: at work, at church, to our MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the shop closes. If AI can run online selling better than any person, Tom's counter can't compete. My job would last a bit longer, because the robots come around 2031 and somebody still has to drive to the welfare checks. But the force would cut back the station side, and I'm junior, so I'm not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk to Tom's dad about closing the shop and leasing out the building, so at least it earns rent. I'd cut back on everything: no holiday, the second car gone, Sunday lunches at my parents' instead of out. And we'd put off the baby, maybe for a few years, which would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing the shop is like losing a family member, it's forty years of my husband's family. And my job's only safe for a few years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save everything I can and stay in the police, because that's the steady wage. Maybe Tom gets trained in something with his hands, like fitting kitchens or plumbing, because those last till 2031 as well. After that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom's dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you for forty years, and that it's not Tom's fault. He'd be quiet for a long time, then he'd say at least the building's paid for. That's how that family deals with things.

say: Two years **isn't time** for families and small firms.
Government should offer **loans and training**, not handouts.
She'd say it at **church** and to their MP.
think: She expects **the shop to close** under AI competition.
Her job lasts until **robots around 2031**, but isn't safe.
As a junior she's **exposed** to station cuts.
do: Close the shop and **lease out the building** for rent.
Cut holidays, **the second car** and meals out.
Put off **having a baby** for a few years.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if losing a family member.
S2.quote: Losing the shop is like losing a family member, it's forty years of my husband's family.
fieldNote: Fast AGI means expecting **both incomes** to fall, one quickly.
Turns to a **hands-on trade** for her husband using the robot gap.
Delaying children is the **deepest cost** for her.

steps.text: Close the hardware shop and lease the Station Road building
Sell the second car and stop eating out
Postpone trying for a baby for a few years
Help Tom train as a kitchen fitter or plumber

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room. 2031, then 2034 for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses have five years to change, and they should get help to do it. Things like low-interest loans and short courses, run locally. I'd say the police should plan properly too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the shop as it is now doesn't survive, but something could. If Tom turned it into a repair and fitting business, cutting keys, fixing tools, going out to fit things, that's hands-on and lasts till 2034 at least. My job would be fine for a while, and I'd be more experienced by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd start shifting the shop now, adding a repair counter and a fitting service, and spend some savings on a van. I'd keep saving the rest. And we'd try for a baby next year as planned, because five years is enough to see our way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. It feels like we'd have to work hard, but we could get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Spending savings on a van is a risk. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because doing nothing is the bigger risk. My dad always said you spend money to make money, but carefully. We'd buy a used one, not a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel having a baby with that much change coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but my faith helps. My grandparents had children in harder times than this. And having family around, Tom's parents and mine, means we wouldn't be on our own.

Offer **low-interest loans** and short local courses.
The police should **plan properly** for the change too.

Her own job is **fine for a while**.
do: Add a **repair counter** and fitting service to the shop.
Spend some savings on a **used van**.
Try for **a baby** next year as planned.
feel: Confident **hard work** could get them through.
S3.quote: Doing nothing is the bigger risk. My dad always said you spend money to make money, but carefully.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **reinvent** the shop instead of closing it.
Draws strength from **faith and family** for a baby.

steps.text: Add a key-cutting and tool repair counter to the shop
Keep saving everything not spent on the used van
Try for a baby next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's much easier to think about. We'd have children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for businesses and families to prepare, if people stop pretending it isn't coming. I'd say it in a hopeful way, not a scary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels manageable. Tom has years to change the shop slowly, and I'd have ten years in the police by 2036, with the robots not till 2039. We could have our children, buy a small house and still have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd start trying for a baby in a couple of years, as planned. Tom would slowly add a trade counter for builders and a repair service. I'd use the police AI tools as they came in, once I'd seen them work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a bit like knowing the roof will need replacing. You plan for it, you don't lie awake over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop, a bit, because it was struggling before AI. Ten years doesn't fix the fact that people buy online. But it gives us time to change it ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to have a trade, or something with their hands, as well as school. And faith, and good manners, because those don't go out of date.

She'd say it **hopefully**, not as a scare.
think: Ten years feels **manageable** for the shop to change slowly.
She'd have **ten years in** by 2036, robots not till 2039.
They could have **children and a house**.
do: Start trying for **a baby** in a couple of years.
Help Tom add a **trade counter** and repairs.
feel: Like planning for **a new roof**: no lost sleep.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to have a trade, or something with their hands, as well as school.
fieldNote: The shop's **old struggle** remains her steady background worry.
Her hopes for children centre on **trades and faith**, things she sees as lasting.

steps.text: Start trying for a baby in about two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd lose the shop and maybe my job, and have to put off children. What would help is practical support for small businesses, loans and training, not handouts, and the police being honest about which roles are safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. People think of AI as a job thing, but for us it's forty years of a family's work on one high street. That's not just income, it's who we are.

headlineQuote: People think of AI as a job thing, but for us it's forty years of a family's work on one high street.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** covering the southern suburbs, married to Tom.
Tom runs his family's **hardware shop**, whose takings are falling; she helps on Saturdays.
Traditional and churchgoing; favours **fair competition** and loans over handouts.
Uses AI **now and then**, after seeing it work; plans children in a couple of years.
Her mood tracks **the shop**: uneasy when AI stalls, **alarmed** when fast AGI closes it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, closing the shop and delaying children.
whatWouldHelp: Police **honesty** about which roles are safe.
